related_questions.question: What are the 5 stages of a cold?

text_blocks.snippet: A cold typically progresses through five stages: incubation, early symptoms, peak symptoms, remission, and recovery. The incubation period is when the virus is present but symptoms haven't started. Early symptoms include a scratchy throat or fatigue. Peak symptoms, like a runny nose and cough, are when the virus is most active. Remission is when symptoms start to lessen, and recovery is when the body is almost back to normal, with only mild lingering symptoms potentially remaining.
snippet_highlighted_words: incubation, early symptoms, peak symptoms, remission, and recovery

list.title: 1. Incubation:
list.snippet: This is the time between when you're infected with the cold virus and when symptoms appear. It can last from 12 hours to 3 days, or even up to a week.

list.title: 2. Early Symptoms:
list.snippet: Symptoms like a sore throat, sneezing, and a runny or stuffy nose begin to appear. You may also feel tired or achy.

list.title: 3. Peak Symptoms:
list.snippet: Symptoms intensify and may include a cough, increased congestion, and body aches. This is often when the cold is most contagious.

list.title: 4. Remission:
list.snippet: Symptoms start to subside. You might still have a cough or some congestion, but you're generally feeling better.

list.title: 5. Recovery:
list.snippet: Most symptoms are gone, though some people may experience lingering cough or fatigue for up to two weeks.

text_blocks.snippet: While there's no cure for the common cold, several treatments can help relieve symptoms and make you more comfortable. These include over-the-counter medications, home remedies, and supportive care. Over-the-counter medications like decongestants, antihistamines, and pain relievers can help with congestion, runny nose, and aches. Home remedies like saltwater gargles, humidifiers, and plenty of fluids can also provide relief.
snippet_highlighted_words: over-the-counter medications, home remedies, and supportive care

list.title: Decongestants:
list.snippet: Help relieve nasal and sinus congestion. Examples include pseudoephedrine (Contac Cold 12 Hour® and Sudafed®).

list.title: Antihistamines:
list.snippet: Can help with sneezing and runny nose. Examples include diphenhydramine (Benadryl®).

list.title: Pain relievers:
list.snippet: Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) can help with fever, headaches, and muscle aches.

list.title: Cough suppressants:
list.snippet: Dextromethorphan (Robitussin and Vicks DayQuil Cough®) and codeine can help reduce coughing.

list.title: Expectorants:
list.snippet: Guaifenesin (Mucinex®) can help loosen mucus.
Saltwater gargle: A saltwater gargle (1 teaspoon of salt in a cup of warm water) can help soothe a sore throat.
Humidifier: A humidifier can add moisture to the air, which can help relieve congestion and a dry throat.
Fluids: Staying hydrated is important. Drink plenty of water, juice, or clear broth.
Rest: Getting enough rest is crucial for recovery.
Steam: Inhaling steam from a hot shower or bowl of hot water can help loosen mucus.
Nasal irrigation: Nasal rinses with saline solution can help clear nasal passages.
Honey: For children over one year old, honey can help soothe a sore throat and suppress coughs, according to Texas Children's.

Children: Avoid giving over-the-counter cold and cough medicines to children under 4 years old, says the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Consult a doctor before giving such medications to children ages 4-6.
Side effects: Be aware of potential side effects of over-the-counter medications and follow dosage instructions carefully.
Consult a doctor: If symptoms are severe or persist for more than 10 days, consult a doctor.

text_blocks.snippet: By using a combination of these treatments and supportive care, you can manage your cold symptoms and feel better faster, says Mount Sinai.
